section_plan.title: New Approach Methodologies and the Data They Generate
section_plan.thesis: New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) - in silico models, organoids, organ-on-chip, high-throughput screening - reach usable, sometimes high predictivity for narrow, well-defined endpoints and can displace specific animal tests. But regulatory readiness is contested, readouts are variable, and NAMs generate large, heterogeneous datasets that will re-create the ethical/scientific debt unless they are stewarded to FAIR standards from the outset.

conflicts_to_present.nature: Regulatory readiness of NAMs: proponents assert NAMs are already fit to assure chemical safety in defined settings, whereas an EU endocrine-disruptor review documents continued dependence on animal data to identify adversity - readiness claimed versus readiness demonstrated.

Transformative promise versus adoption reality for microphysiological systems: one frames MPS as already revolutionising drug development and reducing animal use, while an expert workshop notes MPS have not been widely adopted by industry nor reached regulated drug authorisation.

Reproducibility of MPS readouts: an independent robustness study of a liver MPS finds appreciable within- and between-study variability that undercuts high-throughput utility, whereas MPS advocates present the platforms as standardized and predictive - the same reproducibility problem that afflicts animal models.

section_plan.connection_prev: sec-virtual-controls reduced animal use by reusing animal data; this section covers the Replacement route - non-animal methods - and shows that Replacement does not escape the data problem but relocates it to high-dimensional NAM outputs.
section_plan.connection_next: NAM data, VCG data, and FAIR data all fail to be stewarded for the same underlying reason; sec-incentives exposes that reason as the reward system of research, which prices data stewardship at essentially zero.

figure_specs.label: fig:sec06-nam-vs-invivo
figure_specs.argument_supported: Shows NAM assays reach usable-to-high predictivity against in vivo/consensus references for defined endpoints, but each study uses a different endpoint - performance is real yet fragmented.
figure_specs.what_it_reveals: Plotting sensitivity and specificity for five NAM assay types together reveals both that predictivity is respectable and that the endpoints are non-comparable, which is exactly why FAIR standardisation of NAM data matters.
figure_specs.caption_draft: Figure 15. Predictive performance of NAM assays against in vivo or consensus references. Reconstructed-skin genotoxicity (77%/88%, Pfuhler2020), reporter genotoxicity (84.4%/91.2%, Hendriks2024), skin sensitisation (85.0%/68.2%, Corvaro2024), hepatotoxicity spheroids (86%/100%, Sirenko2016), and HTS-based modelling (balanced accuracy 0.55-0.88, Filer2022) show moderate-to-high, endpoint-specific predictivity. Sensitivity and specificity are shown as paired markers; the heterogeneity of endpoints is flagged in the axis notes.

figure_specs.label: fig:sec06-in-silico-performance
figure_specs.argument_supported: Shows in silico/QSAR NAMs reach high accuracy for narrow endpoints, supporting their use for targeted Replacement while underscoring endpoint fragmentation.
figure_specs.what_it_reveals: A common accuracy axis across three distinct in silico endpoints makes the 'high but narrow' pattern legible and motivates the call for standardised, FAIR NAM outputs that could be pooled.
figure_specs.caption_draft: Figure 16. Predictive accuracy of in silico/QSAR NAMs across endpoints. Derek Nexus phototoxicity (77%, Ahuja2024), a QSAR pregnancy-category model (94.11% external accuracy, KelleciCelik2022), and interspecies aquatic QSAR-ICE models (>75% cross-validation success, Hong2022) demonstrate usable predictivity for well-defined endpoints. Different endpoints and metrics are labelled per bar; a common 100% reference line is shown.

figure_specs.label: fig:sec06-nam-data-scale
figure_specs.argument_supported: Establishes that NAMs generate large, heterogeneous datasets, so Replacement relocates rather than removes the stewardship debt - the same reuse failure will recur unless NAM data are made FAIR.
figure_specs.what_it_reveals: Summarising the scale of curated NAM resources (100,000+ substances; 2,000+ nanomaterials) makes concrete that a new data-welfare debt is being created in non-animal research right now.
figure_specs.caption_draft: Figure 17. Scale of curated NAM/chemical data resources built for reuse. FAIR-oriented resources aggregate >100,000 substances (MohammedTaha2022), >2,000 nanomaterials (Afantitis2020), and 25 meta-analysed proteomic datasets (Bahl2023). NAMs replace animals but generate high-dimensional data that will incur a new ethical and scientific debt unless stewarded to FAIR standards. A log scale is used; exact counts are labelled.

declared_nominal.meaning: Declared / stated / nominal values (data-availability statements, DMP compliance, pledged sharing)

actual_verified.meaning: Actual / verified / usable values (data truly available, FAIR-compliant)

debt_loss_negative.meaning: Data waste, bias inflation, loss, non-reproducibility - the debt

figure_style_guide.redundant_cues_note: Never encode meaning by hue alone. Pair every colour with a second channel: hatch/pattern fills for declared vs actual (open hatch vs solid), distinct markers (circle/triangle/square) on forest and line plots, direct value labels on every bar, and short text annotations naming the focal contrast. Palette is the Okabe-Ito colourblind-safe set; verify with a deuteranopia/protanopia simulation before export.

recurring_themes: The declared-versus-actual gap: across FAIR audits, incentive studies and governance evaluations, stated intent (data-availability statements, DMP compliance, sharing pledges) vastly exceeds usable reality; recurs in sec-fair-preclinical, sec-incentives and sec-governance.
Convergence on ~2% actual data availability as the empirical anchor of the whole review, replicated across specialties and methods.
Reuse as Reduction: reusing existing data (historical/virtual controls, shared datasets, NAM outputs) is framed throughout as a direct 3Rs Reduction dividend, not merely good data hygiene.

False-consensus risk: several field-defining figures (11%/25% industry irreproducibility, US$28B/year, '85% of research wasted') rest on non-transparent or modeled sources and are flagged wherever cited.
Enforcement beats endorsement: passive publication of guidelines rarely changes behaviour; mandated, checked requirements do - a thread from sec-data-welfare through sec-incentives to sec-governance.
The animal-welfare stake: every data-stewardship failure is repeatedly tied back to its cost in animal lives, keeping the ethical argument foregrounded over the purely technical one.

Method-dependence of headline numbers: the same phenomenon (publication rate, concordance, QRP prevalence, sharing trend) yields very different values by method, so juxtaposition rather than single figures is the analytical style.

terminology.ethical_debt: The obligation incurred when animals are used to generate knowledge but the resulting data are allowed to become unfindable, unusable, or unreused; unpaid, it is discharged in further animal lives. Coined and used as the review's organising metaphor.
terminology.data_welfare: The claim that stewardship of animal-derived data (findability, reusability, complete reporting) is a dimension of animal welfare and of the 3Rs, because wasting the data wastes the welfare cost that produced it.
terminology.FAIR: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable - the Wilkinson et al. (2016) principles for machine-actionable data stewardship. Distinguish FAIR (a stewardship standard) from 'open' (an access status); data can be FAIR without being fully open.
terminology.three_Rs: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement (Russell & Burch) - the ethical/legal framework for humane animal research. The review argues data welfare extends all three, chiefly Reduction and Refinement.
terminology.VCG: Virtual Control Group - a control arm reconstructed from curated historical control-animal data to partially or wholly replace concurrent controls, reducing control-animal use. Related term HCD = historical control data.
terminology.NAM: New Approach Methodology - non-animal methods (in silico/QSAR models, organoids, organ-on-chip/microphysiological systems, high-throughput screening) used to predict toxicity or biology; serve Replacement but generate data needing stewardship.
terminology.reproducibility_vs_replicability: Reproducibility = obtaining consistent results using the same data and analysis; replicability = obtaining consistent results in a new study with new data. The review uses 'reproducibility crisis' broadly but distinguishes the two where the evidence does (e.g., direct-replication projects test replicability; re-analysis disputes test reproducibility).
terminology.HBA: Harm-Benefit Analysis - the project-level weighing of animal harm against expected benefit that anchors animal-research regulation; its objectivity and predictive validity are contested.
terminology.QRP: Questionable Research Practice - selective reporting, p-hacking, undisclosed flexibility short of outright fabrication; a behavioural driver of the crisis.
terminology.ARRIVE: Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments - the reporting guideline whose adherence and enforcement are evaluated in sec-governance.

cross_cutting_elements.voice_tone: Critical, evidence-anchored, and quantitative, but ethically serious rather than polemical. Foreground effect sizes and their provenance; state uncertainty and flag false-consensus risks explicitly rather than smoothing them over. Prefer juxtaposition of divergent estimates to single headline numbers. Keep the animal-welfare stake visible without moralising. Third person, present tense for findings; hedged claims ('the evidence suggests', 'audits converge on') proportional to evidence strength.
